item.title: Agent who defrauded landlords and tenants of almost £50,000 learns fate in court
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A former letting agent from Norfolk has been handed a suspended prison sentence after admitting to defrauding landlords and tenants of nearly £50,000. Victoria Steele, 51, who operated Swaffham-based E-HOMES Ltd, formerly known as Prestige Property Ltd, pleaded guilty to 19 counts of fraud. Her actions left 20 victims facing combined losses of £48,858.10.

Details of the Fraud

Steele’s offences included failing to protect tenants’ deposits in a government-backed scheme and withholding rental payments from landlords. Norwich Crown Court heard that her fraudulent activities caused significant financial strain for both parties, with landlords becoming liable for returning deposits despite not receiving the funds. Complaints from landlords and tenants prompted a police investigation, which uncovered the extent of Steele’s misconduct.

The lettings agency closed its Swaffham office in 2018, and the company was officially dissolved in April 2019, according to Companies House records. Victims have waited years for the case to reach its conclusion, with some expressing frustration at the prolonged legal process. Clive Norman, one of the affected landlords, noted that some victims had passed away or moved on during the nine-year wait for justice.

Sentencing and Ongoing Efforts

On 30 September, Steele was sentenced to 12 months in prison, suspended for 18 months, and ordered to complete 200 hours of unpaid work. The court also scheduled a confiscation hearing for February 2027 under the Proceeds of Crime Act, as authorities continue efforts to recover the lost funds and compensate victims.

DC Stuart D’Costa, who led the investigation, emphasised the breach of trust involved in the case. “Steele was entrusted to manage properties and finances professionally, but instead, she abused that trust, leaving her victims significantly out of pocket and enduring prolonged stress,” he said. He also thanked those who came forward to assist in the complex investigation.

This case serves as a reminder of the importance of due diligence when selecting letting agents. Landlords and tenants may wish to verify that their deposits are protected in a government-backed scheme and ensure that payments are being handled transparently. Whilst Steele’s sentence marks a step towards justice, the lengthy process highlights the challenges victims face in recovering lost funds.

item.title: Former estate agents launch rival to LinkedIn and Facebook
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

In a bid to revolutionise networking for UK property professionals, former estate agents Chris and David Tremlett have launched a new platform designed specifically for the industry. Their app, Gatha, aims to provide an alternative to mainstream social media sites like LinkedIn and Facebook, which they argue are not tailored to the needs of property experts. The platform is free to use and focuses on connecting estate agents, landlords, developers, investors, and tradespeople through a dedicated network.

A Dedicated Space for Property Professionals

Gatha was created to address the challenges faced by property professionals who rely on mainstream social media platforms to promote their businesses. The Tremlett brothers highlight that algorithms and paid advertising on these platforms often dictate who sees industry content, making it difficult for smaller firms to compete for visibility. Gatha organises content based on users’ professional roles and geographical locations, rather than follower counts, ensuring that independent agents can reach relevant local audiences without needing to pay for promotions.

The app also features specialised tools, such as a jobs board that connects tradespeople and developers directly, eliminating recruitment fees. Additionally, a projects board allows users to advertise development opportunities and properties seeking investment, with categories including buy-to-let, HMOs, and student accommodation. Members can also communicate with each other through direct messaging, fostering collaboration within the industry.

Challenges of Mainstream Platforms

Chris Tremlett, co-founder of Gatha, explained the frustrations that inspired the platform’s creation. “David and I were estate agents. We know what it’s like to post about a property, a deal, or a job and watch it disappear because you didn’t pay to boost it,” he said. “LinkedIn and Facebook were never built for us. They were built to sell our attention to advertisers, and the property industry has been paying for the privilege for years.”

The brothers believe that the property sector, which plays a vital role in shaping the UK’s infrastructure, deserves a platform that prioritises its needs. “This industry builds the country. It should not have to beg an algorithm to be heard,” Chris added. By offering a free, industry-specific alternative, Gatha aims to empower property professionals to connect and collaborate more effectively.

How to Access Gatha

Gatha is currently available for free to all property professionals. Agents and other industry members can download the app through the Apple App Store, Google Play, or visit the website at gatha.uk. The platform’s founders are encouraging estate agents, developers, and tradespeople to join and experience a networking solution designed specifically for their needs.

As the property industry continues to evolve, platforms like Gatha could provide a valuable space for professionals to connect, share opportunities, and grow their businesses without the constraints of mainstream social media. For those in the sector, it may be worth exploring this new tool to see how it can enhance their networking efforts.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

North Residential, a Yorkshire-based estate agency, has recently strengthened its new homes division with the appointment of Anne Haggas as head of new homes. Haggas brings extensive experience from her previous role at Savills, where she worked within the residential development and new homes sector. Her new position will see her lead North Residential’s expansion efforts across Yorkshire, focusing on development appraisals, consultancy, and the marketing and sale of new properties.

Expanding Yorkshire’s New-Build Market

Haggas’s appointment aligns with North Residential’s strategy to increase its footprint in Yorkshire’s new-build property market. Speaking about her new role, Haggas highlighted the potential to create a standout New Homes division by leveraging strong developer relationships and a tailored approach to marketing and sales. She emphasised her commitment to collaborating with developer clients to drive growth across the region.

Harlan Pollitt, founder of North Residential, described Haggas’s arrival as a significant milestone for the agency. He praised her deep expertise in the new homes sector and her understanding of Yorkshire’s property market. Pollitt also outlined plans to expand the agency’s new homes operations, with Haggas playing a central role in shaping its future development.

Savills Boosts Cambridge Team

Meanwhile, Savills has appointed Ashley Gale as head of its new homes team in Cambridge. With over two decades of experience in the property sector, Gale joined Savills in 2025 after stints at housebuilders Hopkins Homes and Weston Homes. Since joining the agency, he has worked within its Cambridge residential development sales team, advising developers on marketing strategies and overseeing new homes sales.

Gale’s appointment comes at a time when developers are navigating evolving market conditions in Cambridge and the surrounding areas. Despite broader challenges in the housing market, Gale noted that demand for new homes in the region remains strong. He attributed this resilience to factors such as investment in Cambridge’s life sciences and technology sectors, alongside the presence of major institutions like Addenbrooke’s and Royal Papworth hospitals. Gale also highlighted the anticipated impact of Cambridge South station and AstraZeneca’s investment in the Cambridge Biomedical Campus as drivers of continued demand.

Both appointments underscore the ongoing focus on strengthening new homes divisions in key regions, as agencies aim to capitalise on resilient demand and evolving market dynamics.

item.title: Rightmove makes another AI move with new property search feature
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Rightmove has unveiled a new artificial intelligence (AI) tool designed to streamline the property search process for buyers and renters. The Comparison Assistant, powered by Google Gemini, integrates directly into property search results, allowing users to compare homes side by side without navigating multiple listings. This innovation aims to make the search experience more efficient and tailored to individual needs.

Enhanced Property Comparisons

The Comparison Assistant enables users to ask detailed questions about properties, such as which home is better suited for hybrid working or offers more family-friendly features. It also allows comparisons of outdoor spaces and other criteria like nearby schools, transport links, supermarkets, and home-working facilities. The tool combines data from estate agents, Rightmove’s property listings, Google Maps, Experian schools data, and Land Registry records to provide comprehensive insights. This could help buyers and renters make more informed decisions while highlighting key selling points for agents.

Boosting Engagement and Leads

Rightmove’s existing AI tools have already shown promising results in increasing user engagement. Between February and June, users of the Ask Rightmove Search Assistant spent 40% more time on the portal compared to non-users. They also saved twice as many properties and generated double the number of leads for estate agents. While these figures highlight a correlation between AI use and engagement, it’s important to note they don’t prove causation. Nonetheless, the Comparison Assistant could further enhance these trends by simplifying the decision-making process.

Rollout and Future Developments

The Comparison Assistant is the third feature in Rightmove’s Ask Rightmove programme, following the introduction of the AI Search Assistant in February and the Evaluation Assistant in July. Initially, the tool will be available to a limited group of users before a broader rollout. Tarah Lourens, Rightmove’s Chief Technology and Operations Officer, emphasised the tool’s ability to help movers identify homes that best fit their needs while making property listings more discoverable. Maureen Costello of Google Cloud also highlighted the potential of AI to transform the property search experience.

As AI continues to evolve, tools like Rightmove’s Comparison Assistant could play a significant role in shaping how buyers and renters navigate the property market. Homeowners may wish to explore these innovations to simplify their search and make more informed decisions.

item.title: Buy-to-let returns strengthen as landlords expand property portfolios
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Buy-to-let investors across England and Wales have seen rental yields strengthen over the past year, with eight out of ten regions recording improved returns according to Fleet Mortgages' latest quarterly data. The average yield now stands at 7.9%, up from 7.5% in the same period last year, demonstrating resilience despite ongoing economic pressures facing landlords.

Regional yield variations

Yorkshire and Humberside currently offers the highest average rental yield at 9.3%, showing a notable 1.1 percentage point increase year-on-year. The North East follows closely behind at 9.2%, while the East Midlands saw one of the most significant improvements, rising from 7.5% to 8.4%. Other strong performers include:

  • West Midlands: 8.2% (up from 7.5%)
  • South East: 7.2% (up from 6.5%)
  • Greater London: 6.4% (up from 5.9%)

The only regions experiencing yield declines were the North West (down 0.2 percentage points to 8.3%) and Wales (down 0.7 percentage points to 7.5%), though Wales still maintains relatively strong performance compared to southern regions.

Investment activity trends

Interestingly, the data reveals that higher yields don't always correlate with increased investment activity. Wales recorded the highest proportion of purchase applications at 46% despite its yield decrease, while Yorkshire and Humberside - with the strongest yields - saw purchases account for 43% of applications.

The South West showed particularly interesting movements, with purchase applications rising from 23% to 34% quarter-on-quarter alongside improving yields. London continues to command the highest rents nationally, with average monthly payments reaching £2,597 in Q3 2026 - a significant increase from £2,364 in the previous quarter.

The research also indicates a growing trend towards professional landlords with larger portfolios. The average applicant now owns 18 investment properties compared to 16 a year earlier, suggesting the sector is becoming increasingly dominated by experienced investors.

For those considering buy-to-let investments, these figures highlight the importance of thorough regional research and careful financial planning. While yields have generally improved, local market conditions and investment strategies can significantly impact actual returns.

item.title: Record rents in seven of UK’s nine regions
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Renting in the UK has become increasingly expensive, with room rents hitting a record high of £769 per month in the third quarter of the year. According to recent data, seven out of nine regions across the country have seen rental prices reach unprecedented levels. This surge coincides with a 4.7% drop in rental property supply, adding further pressure to an already competitive market.

Rental Market Trends Across the UK

The rental market has experienced significant changes over the past year, with demand continuing to outstrip supply in many areas. The average monthly cost of renting a room has risen sharply, reflecting the challenges tenants face in securing affordable accommodation. Regions such as London, the South East, and the East of England have been particularly affected, with rents climbing steadily due to high demand and limited availability.

Whilst London remains the most expensive region for renters, other areas are also seeing substantial increases. This trend highlights the growing affordability crisis across the UK, as tenants struggle to keep up with rising costs. The shortage of rental properties has been exacerbated by a combination of factors, including landlords exiting the market and a slowdown in new property developments.

Impact on Tenants and the Housing Market

The rise in rental prices has created significant challenges for tenants, particularly those on lower incomes. Many renters are finding it increasingly difficult to allocate a reasonable portion of their earnings towards housing costs, leaving less disposable income for other essentials. This situation could also have broader implications for the housing market, as potential first-time buyers may find it harder to save for a deposit whilst paying higher rents.

For landlords, the current market conditions may present opportunities, but they also face their own set of challenges. Rising interest rates and stricter regulations have led some property investors to reconsider their portfolios, contributing to the decline in rental supply. Borrowers with buy-to-let mortgages might find themselves navigating a complex landscape, where balancing profitability with affordability becomes increasingly difficult.

As the UK rental market continues to evolve, both tenants and landlords are likely to face ongoing pressures. Policymakers and industry stakeholders may need to address the underlying causes of the supply-demand imbalance to ensure a more sustainable housing market in the future.

item.title: London flats most likely to sell at a loss
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

New research reveals that London flats have become the property type most likely to sell for less than their purchase price, with nearly 40% of resales in the capital recording a loss. The findings from e.surv coincide with slowing house price growth across Great Britain, currently standing at just 1.5% annually.

London flat owners face challenging market conditions

Recent analysis highlights a concerning trend for flat owners in the capital, where 39% of resold properties fetched lower prices than their original purchase value. This figure significantly outpaces the national average, suggesting London's apartment market faces unique pressures.

Several factors may contribute to this phenomenon, including an oversupply of new-build flats in certain areas, changing buyer preferences post-pandemic towards properties with outdoor space, and the ongoing impact of rising mortgage rates on affordability. The capital's property market has traditionally shown resilience, but these figures indicate shifting dynamics for specific property types.

National house price growth continues to slow

The data emerges against a backdrop of cooling price growth across Great Britain, with annual increases slowing to 1.5%. This represents a notable deceleration from previous years and reflects broader economic uncertainties, including higher interest rates and cost-of-living pressures.

Regional variations remain significant, with some areas still experiencing robust growth while others see stagnation or decline. The London market's performance often differs from the rest of the country, with its premium property prices making it particularly sensitive to economic shifts and lending conditions.

Considerations for property owners and buyers

For those currently owning London flats, these findings may prompt a review of selling strategies. Homeowners might consider timing their sale carefully or exploring rental options if selling at a loss proves unappealing. Property investors could reassess their portfolios in light of these shifting market conditions.

Prospective buyers might view this as an opportunity to negotiate more favourable terms, particularly for properties that have been on the market for extended periods. However, thorough research remains essential, as market conditions can vary dramatically between different London boroughs and property types.

While the current data paints a challenging picture for London flats, property markets are cyclical by nature. Those considering their options may benefit from professional advice tailored to their specific circumstances and long-term objectives.

item.title: Liverpool overlooked as buy-to-let investment hotspot
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Liverpool has emerged as a standout location for property investors, boasting impressive statistics that often go unnoticed. With an annual price growth of 8.1%, rising rental demand, and a strong gross yield of 5.8%, the city presents compelling opportunities for buy-to-let investors. Despite these attractive figures, Liverpool remains somewhat overlooked compared to other UK property hotspots.

Why Liverpool Stands Out

Liverpool’s property market has shown consistent growth, with house prices increasing at a rate that outpaces many other regions. The city’s affordability, coupled with its vibrant cultural scene and thriving economy, makes it an appealing destination for both renters and investors. Additionally, rental yields in Liverpool are particularly attractive, offering landlords the potential for steady returns.

The city’s regeneration projects, such as the Liverpool Waters development, have further enhanced its appeal. These initiatives are transforming the urban landscape, creating new opportunities for property investment whilst boosting local employment and infrastructure.

Rising Rental Demand

One of the key factors driving Liverpool’s property market is the increasing demand for rental accommodation. The city’s large student population, coupled with its growing workforce, ensures a steady stream of tenants. This demand, combined with relatively affordable property prices, allows landlords to achieve competitive yields.

item.title: Housing commission sets out a radical new plan
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

A major new housing commission has unveiled ambitious proposals aimed at transforming the UK property market. The Prosper UK report outlines sweeping reforms designed to increase housebuilding, improve affordability and remove obstacles to residential development across the country.

Key recommendations for housing reform

The comprehensive proposals address multiple aspects of the housing crisis. Among the most significant recommendations are measures to streamline planning permissions, which could potentially accelerate construction timelines. The commission also suggests reforms to compulsory purchase orders, aiming to make land assembly more straightforward for development projects.

Other notable proposals include:

  • Incentives for local authorities that meet housing delivery targets
  • New mechanisms to encourage development of brownfield sites
  • Revised density guidelines for urban areas
  • Support for modern methods of construction to boost productivity

Potential impact on affordability and availability

The proposals seek to tackle the persistent shortage of homes that has contributed to rising property prices and rental costs. By addressing systemic barriers to development, the commission aims to create conditions where housing supply can better meet demand.

For prospective buyers and renters, successful implementation could lead to a more balanced market in the longer term. However, housing experts caution that significant challenges remain in translating these ambitious proposals into tangible results, given the complexity of the UK planning system.

Industry reaction and next steps

Initial responses from property professionals have been mixed, with some welcoming the bold vision while others question the practicalities of implementation. Housebuilders have generally welcomed the focus on planning reform, though some have raised concerns about potential impacts on local decision-making.

The commission's report is expected to inform ongoing policy debates, though its recommendations would require government action to become reality. As the housing crisis continues to affect communities nationwide, these proposals add to growing calls for comprehensive reform of England's housing and planning systems.

Homeowners and prospective buyers may wish to monitor how these proposals develop, as they could influence housing market dynamics in the coming years. While immediate changes are unlikely, the report represents a significant contribution to discussions about solving Britain's housing challenges.

item.title: Landlord who never visited rental property ordered to pay £28,500
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A landlord has been ordered to pay £28,500 after failing to address severe hazards at a rental property in County Durham. The case highlights the importance of landlords maintaining safe and habitable conditions for tenants, particularly when vulnerable individuals are involved.

Unsafe Living Conditions

The property in Annfield Plain housed a mother, her newborn baby and a disabled child, who endured significant hardships due to the landlord’s negligence. Inspections by Durham County Council revealed a broken boiler, leaving the family without heating or hot water. Further issues included damp, mould, electrical faults and carbon monoxide hazards, all of which posed serious risks to the tenants’ health and safety.

The council first contacted the landlord, Kristoffer Jon Dalziel, in December 2025 after receiving complaints about the property. Despite initial assurances, Dalziel failed to carry out the necessary repairs. Inspections in February and March 2026 confirmed that the hazards remained unaddressed, prompting the council to issue improvement notices under the Housing Act 2004. These notices required Dalziel to restore heating by late March and complete remaining repairs by April, but no action was taken.

Landlord’s Failures

During court proceedings, it emerged that Dalziel had never visited the property since becoming its landlord, except for a pre-purchase viewing. He claimed that delays in repairs were due to the tenant allegedly refusing access, a claim disputed by the tenant. Additionally, Dalziel had failed to obtain selective licences for the Annfield Plain property and two other rental homes in Stanley, breaching Durham County Council’s licensing scheme introduced in April 2022.

Peterlee Magistrates’ Court found Dalziel guilty of multiple offences. He was fined £7,000 for each of the three unlicensed properties and an additional £5,000 for breaching the improvement notice. The total fines amounted to £26,000, with £500 in costs and a £2,000 victim surcharge, bringing his court bill to £28,500.

Council’s Response

Ted Murphy, building safety and standards manager at Durham County Council, described Dalziel’s lack of action as "shocking." He emphasised that the case underscores the need for robust regulation to protect tenants, particularly vulnerable individuals, from unsafe living conditions. The council’s intervention and subsequent legal action demonstrate its commitment to holding landlords accountable for maintaining habitable properties.

This case serves as a stark reminder to landlords of their legal responsibilities. Ensuring rental properties meet safety standards is not only a moral obligation but also a legal requirement. Failure to do so can result in significant financial penalties and reputational damage.

item.title: Rental market takes a turn – but there’s a catch
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Recent data suggests that UK renters may have experienced some relief in September, as rental prices dipped across most regions. However, affordability challenges persist, with significant variations between areas. According to Propertymark, average rents fell in 10 out of 11 regions surveyed, marking a potential shift in the rental market. While this trend could offer a glimmer of hope for tenants, the broader picture highlights ongoing pressures in many parts of the country.

Regional Rental Declines

Scotland saw the most substantial monthly drop, with average rents decreasing by 3.4% to £1,134. The North West followed closely, recording a 2.5% decline to £1,109. London and the South West also experienced reductions, with rents falling by 2.1% in both regions. Meanwhile, the East Midlands bucked the trend, with a marginal 0.1% increase to £991. These figures indicate that while rental prices are cooling in many areas, the extent of the decline varies significantly.

Despite these monthly reductions, annual comparisons reveal a more complex story. Scotland, for example, recorded the largest rise in the income needed to rent, up 3.4% to £34,020. This suggests that while rents may have fallen in the short term, affordability has not necessarily improved for tenants over the past year.

Affordability Challenges Persist

London remains the UK’s most expensive rental market, with average monthly rents at £2,415. To meet Propertymark’s affordability threshold, tenants would need an annual income of £72,450. The South East follows as the second priciest region, with average rents of £1,491 and an indicative income requirement of £44,730. In contrast, the North East offers the lowest average rents at £872, though affordability pressures have increased, with income requirements rising by 1.5% to £26,160.

Some regions, however, have seen improvements. Yorkshire and Humberside recorded the largest annual reduction in income needed to rent, down 3.6% to £28,830. The North West also saw a 2% decrease to £33,270. These figures highlight the regional disparities in affordability, with some areas experiencing relief while others face growing challenges.

The Need for Long-Term Solutions

Kim Lidbury, president of ARLA Propertymark, noted that whilst the September figures indicate some easing of pressure in the rental market, affordability remains a mixed picture. She emphasised the importance of increasing rental supply and retaining landlords in the sector to address these challenges. “A monthly fall in rents does not necessarily mean renting has become more affordable,” Lidbury explained. “Supporting landlords and boosting supply will be crucial to creating a sustainable rental market.”

In summary, whilst recent declines in rental prices may offer short-term relief for tenants, affordability remains a pressing issue in many regions. Borrowers and renters alike might consider exploring their options carefully, keeping in mind the varying dynamics across the UK’s rental market.

item.title: Prime property prices fall further as buyers gain the upper hand
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Prime property prices in the UK have continued their downward trend, with homeowners and buyers navigating a shifting market landscape. According to the latest data from Savills, prime central London property values fell by 1.5% between July and September, contributing to an annual decline of 4.8%. This marks a significant drop from the peak prices seen in 2014, with current values now 27% lower. Meanwhile, prime outer London properties also experienced a quarterly decline of 1.1%, alongside an annual drop of 3% – the steepest in over eight years.

Market Adjustments and Buyer Activity

Despite the ongoing price reductions, there are signs that sellers are adapting to market conditions. More realistic asking prices appear to be encouraging transactions, particularly in higher-value segments. Data from TwentyCi reveals that agreed sales for properties priced above £1m and £2m reached 94% of their levels compared to the same period last year. This suggests that buyers, particularly those with a clear need to move, are taking advantage of the current market dynamics.

Frances McDonald, director of research at Savills, noted that whilst prices in prime central London continue to adjust, activity remains steady. She highlighted that concerns surrounding the upcoming Budget are less pronounced than they were a year ago, contributing to a more stable environment. Cash buyers and those less affected by rising mortgage rates are also playing a key role in supporting transactions.

The Impact of Price Thresholds

The proposed High Value Council Tax Surcharge is adding a layer of uncertainty, particularly for properties at the upper end of the market. Savills’ data shows that outer London houses valued at £2m or more fell by 2.5% annually, compared to a smaller decline of 1.3% for properties below £1m. A similar trend has emerged in prime regional markets, where higher-end properties saw a 5.5% annual decline, whilst homes below £1m experienced a more modest 2.9% drop.

McDonald emphasised the growing sensitivity to price thresholds, with £2m representing both a financial and psychological dividing line for buyers. She suggested that a sustained return to price growth would likely require greater market certainty. Until then, transactions are expected to remain driven by those with a pressing need to move.

Regional Variations in the Market

Prime regional property values also felt the pressure, declining by 1.5% during the quarter and 4.1% annually. However, some areas proved more resilient than others. The Midlands, North of England, Scotland, and Wales recorded quarterly price falls of less than 1%. In contrast, London’s commuter belt and the wider South of England experienced more pronounced declines.

As the market continues to adjust, homeowners may wish to carefully consider pricing strategies to attract motivated buyers. With activity concentrated among those with a clear need to move, setting realistic expectations could be key to securing transactions in the current climate.

item.title: The portfolio case for owning luxury real estate in both Miami and New York
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

For high-net-worth individuals considering international property investments, the debate between Miami and New York often takes centre stage. However, for some buyers, the question isn’t about choosing one over the other but rather how both cities can complement each other within a diverse property portfolio. Luxury real estate in these iconic locations offers unique benefits, and owning in both could present a strategic opportunity for those looking to balance growth, stability, and lifestyle.

The Appeal of Miami and New York

Miami and New York represent two distinct yet equally compelling markets. Miami is renowned for its year-round sunshine, waterfront properties, and thriving luxury lifestyle scene. It attracts buyers seeking a blend of relaxation and investment potential, particularly in the high-end condo market. Meanwhile, New York remains a global financial hub, offering unparalleled cultural experiences, prestige, and a robust real estate market that has historically shown resilience even during economic downturns.

For investors, Miami’s lower tax environment and growing tech sector make it an attractive option, while New York’s status as a global city ensures long-term demand for prime real estate. Together, these cities provide a balance of stability, growth, and diversification, appealing to those looking to maximise their portfolio’s potential.

Strategic Benefits of Owning in Both Cities

Owning luxury properties in both Miami and New York can offer several strategic advantages. Firstly, diversification reduces risk. Whilst New York’s market is often seen as a safe haven, Miami’s growth potential can provide higher returns. Secondly, the lifestyle benefits are significant. A New York penthouse can serve as a base for business and cultural pursuits, whilst a Miami retreat offers a sunny escape. This dual ownership caters to both professional and personal needs.

Additionally, currency fluctuations and geopolitical factors can impact international investments. Holding assets in two major US cities can help mitigate these risks, providing a hedge against uncertainty. For those with a long-term wealth strategy, this approach ensures flexibility and adaptability in changing market conditions.

Considerations for International Buyers

For UK-based buyers, investing in US luxury real estate requires careful planning. Factors such as exchange rates, tax implications, and financing options should be thoroughly researched. Working with experienced international property specialists and mortgage advisors can help navigate these complexities. It’s also worth considering the legal and regulatory differences between the UK and the US, particularly regarding property ownership and inheritance laws.

Mortgages for international properties may differ from domestic loans, and buyers might explore options such as US dollar-denominated mortgages or leveraging existing assets to fund purchases. Ensuring a clear understanding of all costs, including maintenance, management fees, and local taxes, is essential to make informed decisions.

For those considering luxury real estate investments, Miami and New York offer a compelling combination of opportunities. Diversifying across these two markets could provide both financial and lifestyle benefits, making it a strategy worth exploring for high-net-worth individuals. As with any significant investment, thorough research and professional advice are key to achieving the best outcomes.

item.title: Regulation and redress must work hand in hand if this reform is to deliver for consumers
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Effective regulation in the property sector plays a crucial role in protecting consumers while maintaining professional standards. When implemented correctly, it creates a fair marketplace, builds trust, and ensures accountability. However, regulators often face high expectations from the public while navigating complex relationships with industry professionals. The recent government proposal to introduce independent regulation for property agents marks a significant step forward in raising standards across the sector.

The importance of regulation and consumer expectations

item.title: Student lets and Ground 4A: using holding deposits to reserve properties early
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The Renters Rights Act 2025 has introduced significant changes for student landlords in England, particularly around tenancy agreements and early termination. With the removal of section 21 'no fault' evictions and new restrictions on rent payments in advance, many landlords are exploring alternative approaches – including the strategic use of holding deposits to secure student properties earlier in the academic cycle.

New challenges for student landlords

The legislation presents two main difficulties for those letting to students. Firstly, landlords can no longer request multiple months' rent upfront as security, potentially increasing financial risk. Secondly, students can now serve just two months' notice to quit, potentially leaving landlords with voids during term time if replacement tenants aren't found.

Whilst Ground 4A was introduced as a specific possession ground for student tenancies, its usefulness is limited. The provision only applies where the tenancy duration is six months or less – conflicting with the traditional academic year lettings that both students and landlords typically prefer.

The holding deposit solution

Some landlords have considered creative workarounds like unsigned tenancy agreements or 'agreement to let' documents, but these approaches may invalidate Ground 4A rights. A more compliant solution lies in properly structured holding deposits.

Current regulations permit holding deposits of up to one week's rent, even for joint student tenancies. Crucially, the standard 15-day holding period can be extended by written agreement. This allows landlords to:

  • Secure properties for students many months in advance
  • Avoid creating a binding tenancy agreement prematurely
  • Maintain eligibility to use Ground 4A if needed

For example, a landlord negotiating with students in October for a July tenancy start could set a holding deposit deadline in January – creating a reservation period without establishing a full tenancy.

Key considerations

When using extended holding deposits, landlords should ensure:

  • The holding deposit agreement clearly states it doesn't create a tenancy
  • Any extended deadline is properly documented
  • The deposit amount never exceeds one week's rent
  • Standard deposit protection rules are followed

With careful planning, holding deposits can help bridge the gap between student renting patterns and the new regulatory framework, whilst protecting landlords' interests within the law.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Two prominent UK property firms have announced significant leadership changes this month, with Knight Frank promoting a long-standing partner and Vistry Partnerships preparing for a senior retirement after four decades in the sector.

Knight Frank elevates Islington veteran

Sophie McCarthy has been appointed as head of sales at Knight Frank's Islington office, where she has worked since the branch first opened in 2012. The newly-promoted partner brings 17 years of experience with the agency, having begun her career in the firm's St John's Wood branch before helping establish the Islington operation.

In her elevated role, McCarthy will oversee residential sales across the North London office while collaborating with regional partners and Knight Frank's wider London network. The estate agent highlighted her deep understanding of Islington's property market and proven track record in client relationship building as key factors in the appointment.

The promotion reflects Knight Frank's strategy of developing internal talent, with regional partner Jon Reynolds praising McCarthy's "outstanding results" and market expertise. Industry observers may view this as a stabilising move amid fluctuating London property prices, ensuring continuity of service in a competitive local market.

Vistry prepares for leadership transition

Meanwhile, Vistry Group has announced the planned retirement of partnerships chief Stephen Teagle after 40 years in the housing sector. Catherine Raynsford, currently at Legal & General Affordable Homes, will succeed him as group partnerships director from January 2027.

Teagle will remain during the first quarter of next year to oversee the transition before departing at the end of March. His career has spanned both housing associations and plc housebuilders, including 18 years at Galliford Try before its housing operations merged with Bovis Homes to form Vistry.

This leadership change follows earlier appointments at the £4bn-turnover housebuilder, including a new chair in March and group chief executive in April. The transition comes as Vistry navigates a challenging period, having recently reported substantial losses amid broader sector pressures.

For homeowners and investors tracking the UK property sector, these high-profile moves highlight how established firms are balancing continuity with fresh leadership perspectives during a period of economic uncertainty. Both appointments suggest a focus on maintaining strong client relationships while adapting to evolving market conditions.

item.title: Housing market faces fresh squeeze as mortgage rates hit three-year high
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK housing market is currently navigating a challenging period, with falling house prices, rising mortgage rates, and political debates over property taxation creating uncertainty for buyers and sellers alike. Recent data highlights a slowdown in activity, with mortgage approvals and transactions below their long-term averages, whilst borrowing costs have reached their highest levels in three years.

Mortgage Rates Hit Three-Year High

Mortgage rates have surged in recent months, with the average five-year fixed rate reaching 6% in October, its highest level since September 2023, according to Moneyfacts. This increase has been driven by rising inflation expectations, partly linked to geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. Mortgage offers typically last for up to six months, meaning the full impact of higher rates is gradually filtering through to the market.

Bank of England figures reveal that mortgage approvals in August were 14% below their five-year average, suggesting a slowdown in buyer activity. Similarly, HMRC data shows property transactions remained broadly flat compared to historical benchmarks. Experts warn that transaction numbers could decline further in the final months of the year as more borrowers face higher borrowing costs.

Political Uncertainty Adds to Market Challenges

Political debates over property taxation are adding another layer of uncertainty to the market. The Conservative Party has pledged to scrap the proposed council tax surcharge on homes valued at £2 million or more, whilst also announcing plans to abolish inheritance tax on primary residences. In contrast, Labour is advocating for higher taxes on expensive properties, whilst Reform UK opposes new taxes without committing to reverse the surcharge.

These competing policies are particularly affecting the upper end of the market, where buyers and sellers are facing increased uncertainty. With the Budget approaching, the future of property taxation remains unclear, potentially impacting market confidence further.

What Does This Mean for Homebuyers?

For those considering entering the housing market or remortgaging, the current environment presents both challenges and opportunities. Whilst higher mortgage rates may increase borrowing costs, falling house prices could provide some relief for buyers. Homeowners may wish to explore their options carefully, seeking advice to understand how rising rates and political changes could affect their financial plans.

As inflation concerns persist, borrowing costs are likely to remain elevated in the near term. Market analysts have noted that attention has shifted from crude oil supplies to shortages of refined products, particularly diesel, which could further impact inflation and, in turn, mortgage rates.

In summary, the UK housing market is facing a complex mix of economic and political factors, creating a cautious outlook for the remainder of the year. Borrowers and homeowners may need to stay informed and consider their options carefully in this evolving landscape.

item.title: Property consultancy moves office as it plans further hires
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Bradley Hall has recently relocated its Manchester operations to new, larger premises on King Street as part of plans to expand its property consultancy team. The move follows significant growth in the firm's valuation services and will provide capacity for further recruitment across both residential and commercial property sectors.

Expanding team and services

The Manchester office, serving Greater Manchester and surrounding counties including Cheshire and Lancashire, has already welcomed three new surveyors to its ranks. Recent appointments include graduate surveyor Sienna Baker, associate director Benjamin Riddle and chartered surveyor Matthew Beswick. Further recruitment is expected in the coming months as the firm capitalises on growing demand for valuation services.

The consultancy provides a comprehensive range of property services including residential and commercial valuations, working with lenders, developers and private clients. Its broader operations span estate agency, lettings, auctions and property management across 13 UK offices.

Strategic growth in the North West

Charlotte Williams, associate director leading the Manchester team, noted the relocation marks an important milestone in the office's development. The new premises offer improved collaborative spaces and room for expansion while serving an increasing client base across the region.

Neil Hart, Bradley Hall's chief executive, emphasised the firm's people-focused growth strategy. The enhanced facilities are designed to support recruitment of skilled surveyors while meeting rising demand for valuation services in both residential and commercial markets.

Founded in 1988, Bradley Hall has evolved from its North East origins to become a national property consultancy. Its Manchester expansion reflects the firm's commitment to strengthening its presence in key regional markets, with particular focus on valuation services that support lending decisions and property transactions.

For homeowners and property professionals in the North West, the firm's growth may signal increased local capacity for valuation and surveying services. Those requiring property valuations might find it worthwhile researching local providers with expanding teams and specialist expertise in their area.

item.title: Landlord Law Newsround #457
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK’s private rented sector is undergoing significant changes, with new developments and challenges emerging for landlords and tenants alike. From regulatory updates to shifting tenant demographics, here’s a closer look at the latest trends shaping the property market.

New PRS Ombudsman Scheme Expected by 2028

The introduction of a compulsory Private Rented Sector (PRS) Landlord Ombudsman has been confirmed, with the scheme anticipated to launch in 2028. While the Government has yet to select an operator for the service, it is expected that nearly all private landlords will be required to join. This new initiative is separate from the existing voluntary membership offered by the Housing Ombudsman. The move aims to improve accountability and dispute resolution within the rental market, offering tenants greater protection and landlords clearer guidelines.

Rising Demand for Out-of-Hours Tenant Support

Recent research highlights a growing trend of tenants reaching out to landlords and letting agents outside standard working hours. According to LightWork AI, 43% of tenant communications now occur outside the traditional 9am to 5pm window, with 49% being emails or portal enquiries and 28% phone calls. This shift places additional pressure on agents and landlords, who are increasingly expected to be available around the clock. Leonard Charlton, co-founder of LightWork AI, noted that this constant demand is contributing to burnout within the industry, making it harder to retain skilled professionals.

Changing Tenant Demographics and Aspirations

The profile of the average tenant is evolving, with many renters facing barriers to homeownership. A survey by the TDS Charitable Foundation reveals that 76% of renters aspire to buy their own home, yet 44% now expect to rent for the rest of their lives. This has led to longer tenancies, with the average duration now standing at 4.7 years, up from 3.7 years a decade ago. Additionally, there is growing interest in social housing, particularly among older tenants, families, and those with health conditions. The findings underscore the need for housing policies to adapt to these shifts, ensuring renters have access to a wider range of options beyond private renting.

Energy Efficiency Concerns in the Rental Market

Energy efficiency is becoming a key consideration for tenants, with 42% factoring it into their rental decisions. However, many landlords are struggling to meet EPC (Energy Performance Certificate) targets, particularly as the Government pushes for greener housing standards. This gap highlights the challenges faced by landlords in upgrading properties to meet evolving expectations, while tenants increasingly prioritise sustainability and cost-saving measures.

As the rental market continues to evolve, landlords, tenants, and policymakers alike will need to navigate these changes to ensure a fair and sustainable future for the sector.
